| [LIT-445](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-445.md) | From the Phenomenology to the Mechanisms of Consciousness: Integrated Information Theory 3.0 | Oizumi, Albantakis & Tononi (2014), PLoS Computational Biology 10(5):e1003588. IIT 3.0 states five axioms of experience (existence, composition, information, integration, exclusion), turns each into a postulate about mechanisms in a state, and identifies an experience with the maximally irreducible conceptual structure of a "complex". Exclusion makes a complex a local maximum of integrated conceptual information Φ over all overlapping sets of elements, so complexes cannot overlap and no subset or superset of a complex is conscious. Worked logic-gate examples show minor complexes beside a major one, an inactive network that is conscious, a minimally conscious photodiode, and a feed-forward "zombie" functionally equivalent to a conscious system. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-365](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-365.md)), equations excepted; worth reading as the formal statement of the exclusion postulate that Schwitzgebel's 2014 manuscript ([LIT-159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-159.md)) attacks: "of all overlapping sets of elements, only one set can be conscious", a complex being a local maximum of Φ against every overlapping set. It is IIT's anti-nesting principle, stated as a postulate and motivated only by the phenomenological exclusion axiom; the paper's Occam's-razor argument is given for exclusion within a mechanism, not between systems. It also says plainly that function does not fix consciousness, which is IIT's answer to whether agency built from parts brings experience with it. |
| [LIT-453](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-453.md) | Philosophical conceptions of the self: implications for cognitive science | Gallagher (2000), Trends in Cognitive Sciences 4(1):14–21. Divides philosophical accounts of the self into the "minimal self", accessible to present self-consciousness without temporal extension, and the "narrative self", extended in time through memory and story. The minimal self splits into a sense of ownership and a sense of agency, which come apart in involuntary movement and, after Frith, in schizophrenic thought insertion when a forward comparator fails. Neonatal imitation suggests an embodied minimal self; Strawson's and Tani's are momentary. Against Dennett's narrative centre, the self is "the sum total of its narratives". Read in the author's preprint. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-377](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-377.md)), in the author's preprint, not the typeset article; worth reading as the paper that set the minimal self against the narrative self for cognitive science, and for the split of the minimal self into a sense of ownership and a sense of agency, which it ties to Frith's comparator model of schizophrenic thought insertion. It is a short review: the empirical support is cited, not shown, and its own proposal, the self as "the sum total of its narratives", is offered in two paragraphs. |

| [LIT-568](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-568.md) | Précis: Being No One | Metzinger (2005), PSYCHE 11(5), the author's précis of Being No One. Minimal consciousness is a global world-model in a window of presence that cannot be recognised as a model (globality, presentationality, transparency). A phenomenal self is a transparent self-model: "no such things as selves exist in the world". Transparency comes in degrees, and the self-model's opaque partition is what lets humans doubt their own self-representation. The unity of consciousness is a single global functional cluster. A first-person perspective is a phenomenal model of the intentionality relation, and iterating it yields introspective and social intelligence. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-460](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-460.md)), as the read substitute for Being No One ([LIT-467](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-467.md)), which it summarises in Metzinger's own words. Worth reading as the most complete short statement of the self-model theory of subjectivity (SMT): more of the machinery than "Self models" ([LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md)), in particular the six constraints, the degrees of transparency, and the phenomenal model of the intentionality relation (PMIR). Phenomenal selfhood is a transparent self-model, "a function realized by a lack of information"; "no such things as selves exist in the world". The unity of a conscious world is a global functional cluster bound by "highest-order binding". It states the theory and its predictions; the evidence is cited, not shown, and the neural sections say how little is known. |
| [LIT-571](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-571.md) | Participatory sense-making: An enactive approach to social cognition | De Jaegher & Di Paolo (2007), Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences 6(4):485–507. Coordination between coupled systems is cheap and common. When patterns of coordination and the course of an encounter shape each other, the interaction acquires its own operationally closed, precarious organization. Social interaction is then regulated coupling between autonomous agents that constitutes an autonomous relational organization without destroying the agents' autonomy. Because sense-making is embodied in movement, interactors can coordinate their sense-making, along a spectrum from modulated individual sense-making to jointly created meaning. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-456](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-456.md)), from the published version posted on De Jaegher's own site. The argument is conceptual, illustrated by everyday cases and by the perceptual-crossing experiments; nothing is measured in the paper. |

| [LIT-1191](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1191.md) v2 | Towards a computational phenomenology of mental action: modelling meta-awareness and attentional control with deep parametric active inference | Sandved-Smith, Hesp, Mattout, Friston, Lutz & Ramstead (2021). A three-level discrete active-inference model: attentional states (focused, distracted) set the precision of the perceptual likelihood, and meta-awareness states (high, low) set the precision with which the agent observes its own attentional state. Mental action is a policy, 'stay' or 'switch', over attentional states, defined at that level only and driven by a preference to observe oneself 'focused'. Single simulations of a passive oddball reproduce focus, mind-wandering, noticing and refocusing, with longer mind-wandering under low meta-awareness. Stimuli are fixed by the generative process, so mental action changes how strongly they update belief, not what they are; no likelihood is learned. | Active — read 2026-10-16 ([NOTE-958](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-958.md)) in full, from the PubMed Central deposit of the journal version; worth reading as the active-inference model of mental action: attentional states set the precision of the perceptual likelihood, meta-awareness states set the precision of the attentional likelihood, and the agent selects 'stay' or 'switch' over its own attentional state against a preference to observe itself 'focused', reproducing the cycle of focus, mind-wandering and refocusing. Read it knowing that action is defined at the attentional level only; that the agent's attentional state is modelled as a generative process the mental action acts on, so the loop is action and perception one level inward; that the perceptual observations are fixed in advance and mental action changes only their precision; that nothing is learned; and that the results are single illustrative simulations with no data fitted. |

| [LIT-1356](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1356.md) v2 | What Is Enactivism? | Ward (2026). Treating "enactivism" as an umbrella for any view that stresses sensorimotor loops ignores what sets apart the enactive approach of Varela, Thompson and Rosch: life–mind continuity, the primacy of lived experience, and reciprocity between science and self-understanding. A second axis, organicist against informationalist, runs across the cognitivist–embodied one. Embodied predictive processing, extended functionalism and cybernetics are embodied and informationalist; the enactive approach is organicist. A taxonomy, not an argument that organicism is true. | Active — read in full 2026-10-22 ([NOTE-1065](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1065.md)) from the author's accepted manuscript in the University of Edinburgh repository; worth reading as a short, clear map that separates where a view puts cognition's processes (skull, or brain–body–world) from what it says meaning depends on (information, or organization distinctive of living things). On that map embodied predictive processing, extended functionalism and cybernetics are embodied but informationalist, and the enactive approach of The Embodied Mind is organicist, further marked by the primacy of lived experience and by reciprocity, in which the vocabularies we understand ourselves with reshape the experience they describe. Its main limit is that it argues for a taxonomy, not for organicism, and gives no criterion for which properties are distinctive of life. It does not discuss brains in vats, development or grounding. |
| [LIT-1361](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1361.md) v3 | Phenomenal structure: What is it and what is it for? | Isaac (2025). Sets out a structuralist science of phenomenal experience: experience has geometric structure (quality spaces), group-theoretic structure (perceptual constancies, which induce a distinction between subject and object) and dynamical structure (valence and affordance). Its method is to find structure-preserving maps between these and neural and physical structures, made testable because structural relations between experiences show up in behaviour, and evidenced chiefly by convergence between models built from different behavioural procedures, which it concedes is partial. | Active — read in full 2026-10-25 ([NOTE-1163](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1163.md)) from the publisher's gold open-access PDF (version of record, CC BY), which the publisher's site served on 2026-10-25 after refusing every request on 2026-10-22; worth reading as a structuralist programme that, unlike Lyre's ([LIT-1344](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1344.md)), denies that quality-space geometry is enough: it adds constancy as invariance under transformations within experience, which after Cassirer it takes to make experience objective and to separate subject from object ([THEORY-959](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-959.md)), and fields of valence and affordance; and for its account of how a third-personal science reaches experience, chiefly by convergence between models built from different behavioural procedures ([THEORY-953](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-953.md)). Read it knowing that it is programmatic and tests nothing, that the author calls the group-theoretic and dynamic layers "mere suggestive sketches", that "group-theoretic" is used for invariance in general (its own examples are groupoids or toy models), that it gives no criterion separating a subject–object distinction from mere invariant extraction, that the convergence it cites is coarse and its argument does not exclude a shared stimulus geometry as the common factor, and that, like Lyre, it addresses the character of experience, not whether a state is conscious. |
| [LIT-1721](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1721.md) | Being one of us: we-identities and self-categorization theory | León (2023). A we-identity is one a subject has as a group member, is at times aware of, endorses, and cares about. But the we-identities of close relationships arise by mutual individualization: partners grasp each other as non-substitutable and complementary. | [LIT-1758](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1758.md) | Second-Person Engagement, Self-Alienation, and Group-Identification | Zahavi (2016/2019) reconstructs and defends Husserl's empathy-based account of the "we" against Heidegger and Hans Bernhard Schmid. Truly social acts need a second-person relation: an I–Thou relation of reciprocal, communicative address, in which I am aware of the other and of myself as addressed by them. Taking over the other's perspective on oneself, a self-apprehension Husserl calls "self-alienation", lets the difference between self and other stay present but be "somewhat downplayed", and that is a formal condition of coming to see oneself as "one of us". A we is "not an enlarged I": it preserves plurality and is not fusion. Zahavi likens the condition to self-categorization theory's self-stereotyping, while noting that Husserl attends far more to the interpersonal encounter beneath it. Against Schmid he argues that the sense of "us" can be analysed, that not every social relation is a we, and that children's self-awareness precedes their in-group bias. He concedes that an account built on the dyadic face-to-face "we" does not cover anonymous, institutional "we"s. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1289](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1289.md)) from the peer-reviewed accepted manuscript in the University of Copenhagen's repository (curis.ku.dk); worth reading as the phenomenologist's case that coming to see oneself as one of us is a change in how one apprehends oneself, through another's eyes, and that the resulting "we" is a plurality, not an enlarged I. |
